items.title: The Economics of Environmental Degradation
items.body:
## Forms of degradation

- **Deforestation**, **air/water/soil pollution**, **soil degradation & desertification**, and **loss of biodiversity** are the principal forms of environmental degradation — the deterioration of the environment through depletion of resources and ecosystem destruction.

## Why markets fail the environment

- **Negative externality:** pollution imposes a cost on third parties that the producer does not pay, so **social cost > private cost** and the polluting good is **overproduced** relative to the social optimum.
- **Public goods** (clean air) are non-excludable and non-rival, so markets under-provide them.
- **Tragedy of the commons (Garrett Hardin, 1968):** open-access common-pool resources (fisheries, grazing land, air) are overused because each user gains privately while depletion costs are shared.
- **Environmental Kuznets Curve (EKC):** an **inverted-U** — degradation first rises with per-capita income, peaks, then falls as richer societies demand and can afford cleaner technology and regulation.
keyPoints: Main forms of degradation: deforestation, pollution (air/water/soil), soil degradation/desertification, biodiversity loss.
A negative externality means social cost exceeds private cost, causing overproduction of the polluting good.
Tragedy of the commons (Hardin, 1968): open-access shared resources are overused.
Environmental Kuznets Curve is an inverted-U between per-capita income and degradation.
Environmental goods fail in markets because they are externalities, public goods or common-pool resources.
items.mnemonic: Degradation = 'DPSB' — Deforestation, Pollution, Soil/desertification, Biodiversity loss.
items.source: NCERT Introductory Microeconomics; Britannica — externalities, commons, EKC

items.title: Environmental Policy Instruments & Principles
items.body:
## Command-and-control vs market-based

| Type | Examples | Idea |
|---|---|---|
| Command-and-control | Emission standards, bans, licensing, EIA clearance | Direct regulation of what/how much can be emitted |
| Market-based | **Pigouvian tax**, **cap-and-trade** (tradable permits), subsidies for clean tech | Put a price on pollution so firms internalise the cost |

- A **Pigouvian tax** sets the tax equal to the marginal external cost, raising private cost to the social cost.
- **Cap-and-trade** fixes a total emissions cap and lets firms trade permits, achieving cuts at least cost.
- The **Coase theorem** notes that with clear property rights and low bargaining costs, parties can negotiate an efficient outcome without government.

## Guiding principles (read into Article 21)

- **Polluter Pays Principle:** the polluter bears the cost of pollution and of restoring environmental damage.
- **Precautionary Principle:** lack of full scientific certainty is no reason to postpone preventive action.
- **Sustainable Development:** meeting present needs without compromising future generations (Brundtland). The Supreme Court in **Vellore Citizens' Welfare Forum v. Union of India (1996)** held these to be part of Indian environmental law.
keyPoints: Policy instruments split into command-and-control (standards, bans, EIA) and market-based (Pigouvian tax, cap-and-trade, subsidies).
A Pigouvian tax equals the marginal external cost; cap-and-trade caps total emissions and allows permit trading.
Coase theorem: clear property rights + low bargaining cost can yield efficiency without regulation.
Polluter Pays and Precautionary principles are part of Indian law via Article 21 (Vellore Citizens case, 1996).
Sustainable development (Brundtland) balances present needs with future generations.
items.mnemonic: Two toolkits: 'CAC' (Command-And-Control) rules vs market prices (tax/trade).
items.source: NCERT; Supreme Court — Vellore Citizens' Welfare Forum v. Union of India (1996)

items.title: Environmental Laws, Institutions & EIA
items.body:
## Key statutes

| Law | Year | Focus |
|---|---|---|
| Wildlife Protection Act | 1972 | Protected areas & species schedules |
| Water (Prevention & Control of Pollution) Act | 1974 | Created **CPCB** & **SPCBs** |
| Forest Conservation Act | 1980 | Restricts diversion of forest land |
| Air (Prevention & Control of Pollution) Act | 1981 | Air-quality control |
| **Environment (Protection) Act** | 1986 | **Umbrella law** after Bhopal (1984) |

## Institutions

- **MoEFCC** — nodal ministry for policy, clearances and international negotiations.
- **CPCB (1974)** & **State Pollution Control Boards** — set/enforce pollution standards.
- **National Green Tribunal (2010)** — specialised tribunal for speedy environmental justice, applying polluter-pays and sustainable-development principles.

## Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA)

- Governed by the **EIA Notification, 2006** (under the EPA 1986).
- **Category A** — appraised centrally by MoEFCC's Expert Appraisal Committee; **Category B** — by State/SEIAA (B1 needs EIA, B2 exempt).
- Four stages: **Screening → Scoping → Public Consultation → Appraisal.** The Draft EIA 2020 (allowing post-facto clearance) was widely criticised.
keyPoints: Chronology: Wildlife 1972, Water 1974, Forest Conservation 1980, Air 1981, EPA 1986 (umbrella, post-Bhopal).
The Water Act 1974 created the CPCB and State Pollution Control Boards.
NGT was established in 2010 for speedy disposal of environmental cases.
EIA is governed by the 2006 Notification under the EPA 1986, with Category A (central) and B (state) projects.
EIA stages: Screening, Scoping, Public Consultation, Appraisal.
items.mnemonic: Law order '72-74-80-81-86' = Wildlife, Water, Forest, Air, Environment.
items.source: MoEFCC — environmental legislation; EIA Notification 2006; NGT Act 2010

items.title: India's Climate Commitments — Paris, Panchamrit & Net-Zero
items.body:
## Paris Agreement & India's NDC

- The **Paris Agreement (COP21, 2015)** commits countries to limit warming well below 2°C via **Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs)**.
- India's **updated NDC (2022)**:
  - Reduce **emissions intensity of GDP by 45%** by 2030 (from 2005 levels) — up from the original 33–35%.
  - Achieve **about 50%** cumulative electric power installed capacity from **non-fossil** sources by 2030 — up from 40%.

## Panchamrit (COP26, Glasgow 2021)

| # | Commitment (by 2030 unless stated) |
|---|---|
| 1 | Non-fossil energy capacity of **500 GW** |
| 2 | **50%** of energy requirements from renewables |
| 3 | Cut carbon intensity by **45%** (vs 2005) |
| 4 | Reduce projected emissions by **1 billion tonnes** |
| 5 | **Net-zero by 2070** |

## Governance architecture

- **NAPCC (2008)** — eight national missions (Solar, Enhanced Energy Efficiency, Sustainable Habitat, Water, Himalayan Ecosystem, Green India, Sustainable Agriculture, Strategic Knowledge).
- **International Solar Alliance** — co-founded by India and France (launched COP21, HQ Gurugram).
- **Mission LiFE (2022)** — 'Lifestyle for Environment', promoting mindful, low-carbon consumption.
keyPoints: India's net-zero target year is 2070 (fifth Panchamrit element, COP26 Glasgow 2021).
Updated NDC 2022: 45% cut in emissions intensity of GDP by 2030 (vs 2005) and ~50% non-fossil power capacity.
Panchamrit 2030 targets: 500 GW non-fossil capacity, 50% renewables, 45% intensity cut, 1 billion-tonne emission cut.
NAPCC (2008) has eight national missions, including the National Solar Mission.
International Solar Alliance was co-founded by India and France; Mission LiFE promotes sustainable lifestyles.
items.source: PIB / UNFCCC — Paris Agreement, India's updated NDC (2022), COP26 Panchamrit; MoEFCC — NAPCC

items.title: Carbon Markets & Green Finance in India
items.body:
## Carbon markets

- A **carbon market** puts a price on emissions, allowing entities to buy/sell the right to emit and cutting emissions at least cost.
- **Compliance markets** are mandatory (targets set by regulation); **voluntary markets** let firms buy credits by choice (CSR, offsets).
- **Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (CCTS), 2023** — notified under the **Energy Conservation Act, 2001 (amended 2022)**; the **Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE)** administers it and the **Grid Controller of India** runs the registry. It has:
  - a **compliance mechanism** (emission-intensity targets for obligated industries), and
  - an **offset mechanism** (voluntary registered projects). The traded unit is the **Carbon Credit Certificate (CCC)**.

## Precursor markets

- **PAT ('Perform, Achieve, Trade')** — BEE energy-efficiency scheme; over-achievers earn **Energy Saving Certificates (ESCerts)** traded on power exchanges.
- **Renewable Energy Certificates (RECs)** — represent the 'green' attribute of renewable electricity.

## Green finance

- **Sovereign Green Bonds** — India issued its first SGrBs in **2022–23 (₹16,000 crore)** to fund solar, wind, green transport and afforestation.
- **Green budgeting** — using the budget process (tagging/allocations) to further environmental goals; practised by several Indian states.
- **Green Credit Programme (2023)** — a market mechanism under the EPA 1986 rewarding voluntary actions such as tree plantation.
keyPoints: CCTS 2023 was notified under the Energy Conservation Act, 2001 (amended 2022); BEE is the administrator.
CCTS has a compliance mechanism (obligated entities) and an offset mechanism (voluntary projects).
Compliance carbon markets are mandatory; voluntary markets are by choice.
PAT scheme issues tradable ESCerts; RECs represent renewable-electricity attributes.
India issued its first Sovereign Green Bonds in 2022–23 (₹16,000 crore); the Green Credit Programme (2023) rewards voluntary green actions.
items.mnemonic: India's carbon-market lineage: PAT (ESCerts) + REC → CCTS (Carbon Credit Certificates).
items.source: Ministry of Power / BEE — CCTS 2023, PAT, REC; RBI — Sovereign Green Bonds; MoEFCC — Green Credit Programme

items.title: Green Accounting & Natural-Capital Accounting
items.body:
## Why green accounting

- Conventional GDP treats the environment as free and can **rise even as forests, water and air quality deteriorate**.
- **Green accounting** corrects this by valuing **natural capital** and the cost of environmental degradation.

## From GDP to Green GDP

| Aggregate | Adjustment |
|---|---|
| GDP | Total output |
| NDP | GDP − depreciation of **man-made (fixed)** capital |
| **Green GDP** | NDP − depletion/degradation of **natural** capital |

## SEEA — the global standard

- **SEEA** (System of Environmental-Economic Accounting) links environmental and economic data; origin in a **1993 SNA satellite handbook**.
- **SEEA Central Framework — 2012** standard; **SEEA Ecosystem Accounting — 2021** standard (UN Statistical Commission).

## India's efforts

- **MoSPI 'EnviStats India'** — published **annually since 2018**, using SEEA (physical + monetary accounts).
- India was a partner country of the **NCAVES project (2017–21)** (EU–UN) on ecosystem accounting.
- **Expert Group under Sir Partha Dasgupta (2013)** gave a 'Green National Accounts in India' framework; the **Dasgupta Review (2021)** reframed the economy as embedded in nature.
- **Uttarakhand** moved to estimate a **Gross Environment Product (GEP)**.

## Related global indicators

- **Adjusted Net Savings / Genuine Savings** — World Bank measure of true saving net of resource depletion and pollution.
- **Inclusive Wealth Index** — UNEP measure of produced, human and natural capital.
- **Ecosystem services** — provisioning, regulating, cultural and supporting (Millennium Ecosystem Assessment).
keyPoints: Green GDP = NDP minus depletion/degradation of natural capital; NDP already nets out fixed-capital depreciation.
SEEA Central Framework became a UN standard in 2012; SEEA Ecosystem Accounting in 2021; origin in the 1993 SNA handbook.
MoSPI publishes 'EnviStats India' annually since 2018 using the SEEA framework.
India was a partner country of the EU–UN NCAVES project (2017–21) on ecosystem accounting.
A Partha Dasgupta Expert Group gave India a Green National Accounts framework in 2013; the Dasgupta Review followed in 2021.
Uttarakhand moved to estimate its Gross Environment Product (GEP).
Adjusted Net Savings (World Bank) and the Inclusive Wealth Index (UNEP) are allied natural-capital indicators.
Ecosystem services: provisioning, regulating, cultural and supporting (Millennium Ecosystem Assessment).
items.source: UN SEEA; MoSPI — EnviStats India; World Bank; UNEP; HM Treasury — Dasgupta Review (2021)
